## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anusāsikajātaka* (Ja 115) is a story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, translated under the title *The Warner*. According to the commentary, the Buddha delivered the tale while staying at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, occasioned by an admonishing nun (*anusāsikā bhikkhunī*) [Fausböll 1877]. Born of a respectable family in Sāvatthī, she became slack in her monastic duties after ordination and grew gluttonous for alms, seeking food in dangerous areas of the city unvisited by other sisters while forbidding them to go there [Fausböll 1877]. When she went thither herself, she had her thigh broken by a fierce ram (*caṇḍa meṇḍaka*) [Fausböll 1877].

After hearing the monks in the Dhammasabhā discussing her misfortune, the Buddha explained that this was not the first time she had warned others while failing to follow her own counsel [Fausböll 1877]. Relating the story of the past (*atītavatthu*) introduced by the verse opening *Yayaññam anusāsati*, the Buddha revealed that she had previously been an admonishing maina bird (*sālikā sakuṇikā*) that greedily scavenged along a carriage road and was crushed by a wheel [Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the greedy bird was identified with the nun, and the chief of the flock (*sakuṇajeṭṭhaka*) was identified with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].
